stories.headline: Trump, Zelensky, and Netanyahu Attend Lindsey Graham's Funeral at Washington National Cathedral
stories.summary:
Senator Lindsey Graham was honored at a state funeral at Washington National Cathedral, with President Trump, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu among the dignitaries in attendance. The service concluded with mourners singing Amazing Grace, and pallbearers carried Graham's casket out to Aaron Copland's Fanfare for the Common Man. Graham's casket is now being transported to South Carolina for additional services and burial.

The gathering of Trump, Zelensky, and Netanyahu at a single ceremony is diplomatically significant, coming amid active U.S. involvement in both the Iran conflict and ongoing deliberations over Ukraine war support. Graham had been a prominent voice in the Senate on both foreign policy fronts throughout his career. The funeral brought together figures whose relationships have been strained by recent geopolitical tensions.

Graham, a Republican from South Carolina who served in the Senate since 2003, was one of the most recognizable figures in American foreign policy circles, known for his hawkish views and close relationships with leaders across the political spectrum. His death leaves a vacancy in a closely watched Senate seat. Further memorial services are planned in South Carolina ahead of his burial.

stories.headline: French Navy Fires Shots During BBC Interview in English Channel, Sparking Diplomatic Row
stories.summary:
A French Navy patrol boat fired approximately 17 rounds in the English Channel while a BBC journalist was conducting a live interview with UK shadow home secretary Chris Philp about small boat migrant crossings. The shots were fired without prior warning to the British vessel, which was approximately 300 meters away and roughly three miles from the French coast. The incident occurred at around 09:15 BST on Monday.

Philp, a Conservative MP, characterized the firing as deliberate intimidation designed to prevent coverage of migrant crossings. 'It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation,' he said, adding that he would raise the matter with the French ambassador. The captain of the fishing boat hosting the interview said he had 'never seen anything like it before.'

French authorities maintained the patrol boat PSP Flamant was conducting a routine individual training exercise unrelated to the presence of the British vessel, and that all required international safety signals had been displayed. A UK government spokesperson said the matter was 'for the French authorities.' The incident is likely to inflame ongoing tensions between Britain and France over Channel migration policy, with Philp arguing that France 'waves through' migrants while actively obstructing British press coverage.

stories.headline: Hong Kong Pro-Democracy Leader Wu Chi-wai Allowed to Stay in UK After Initial Detention at Heathrow
stories.summary:
Former Hong Kong Democratic Party leader Wu Chi-wai, one of the so-called Hong Kong 47 pro-democracy figures, has been granted a standard six-month stay in the United Kingdom after being detained for nearly 10 hours at Heathrow Airport last week and initially told he would be deported within days. UK Border Force reversed course Monday, approving his entry under his British National (Overseas) passport. Wu had sought to reunite with his wife and son, who relocated to the UK in 2022 and 2023 while he was imprisoned.

Wu was sentenced under Hong Kong's national security law and spent more than five years in prison on subversion and related charges before being released in June. He said he had consulted the British Consulate General in Hong Kong before traveling and was told there would be no entry issues, making his initial detention at Heathrow unexpected. The Border Force had initially determined he was not a 'genuine visitor' solely traveling to see family.

Rights group Hong Kong Watch welcomed the reversal but criticized the handling of the case. 'This is the right outcome, and it should never have taken this long,' said policy director Megan Khoo. 'He should never have faced the prospect of removal back to the city that jailed him.' The case highlights ongoing tensions over the UK's obligations to Hong Kong activists under the BNO passport program, which was expanded in 2021 following Beijing's crackdown on the pro-democracy movement.

stories.headline: Consumer Confidence Falls Again as Iran Conflict Pushes Gas Prices to $4.10 a Gallon
stories.summary:
The Conference Board reported Tuesday that its consumer confidence index fell to 90.8 in July from 92.2 in June, extending a prolonged period of economic pessimism. The index has remained in a tepid range throughout 2026, well below readings above 100 recorded in late 2024 and early 2025. The decline comes as gas prices have climbed back to $4.10 per gallon nationally after briefly retreating to approximately $3.70 in June.

The renewed rise in energy costs is directly linked to the escalating U.S.-Iran conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil travels. Iran shut the strait following U.S. and Israeli strikes in late February, causing an initial price spike. A brief period of reduced fighting had allowed some relief at the pump before hostilities intensified again.

Inflation has risen to 3.5% since Trump's inauguration in January 2025, up from 3% at that time, and accelerated further after the Iran war began in February when it stood at 2.4%. Food prices have been a particular source of strain, with groceries 33% more expensive than at the start of 2019 and ground beef averaging $6.82 per pound in June — 79% higher than in early 2019. Survey respondents' mentions of food and grocery prices increased this month.

The persistently sour economic mood carries political implications with midterm elections fewer than 100 days away. President Trump has continued to attribute inflation to his predecessor, former President Biden, while Democrats point to price increases that have occurred during Trump's current term. The employment picture showed mixed signals, with only 57,000 jobs added last month — less than half the prior month's total — though the unemployment rate edged down to 4.2%.

stories.headline: Florida Carries Out Two Executions in a Single Day for First Time in Nearly a Decade
stories.summary:
Florida executed former police officer James Aren Duckett, 68, on Tuesday afternoon for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Teresa McAbee, making him the 11th inmate put to death in the state this year. Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning the girl while on duty as a police officer in central Florida. He declined to make a final statement before his death at 1:19 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke.

Later Tuesday evening, 80-year-old Dominick Anthony Occhicone was scheduled to be executed for the 1986 murders of his ex-girlfriend's parents, which would make him the oldest prisoner executed in Florida's modern history. The two executions in a single day mark the first time any U.S. state has carried out back-to-back executions since Arkansas did so in 2017.

Gov. Ron DeSantis has dramatically accelerated Florida's use of capital punishment over the past 18 months, at a pace not seen in the state since the U.S. reinstated the death penalty in 1976. Florida has accounted for nearly half of all state executions nationwide since the beginning of 2025. Both men had sought last-minute intervention from the U.S. Supreme Court and the Florida Supreme Court, and both were denied.

Duckett's attorneys claimed innocence and argued the state's handling of DNA evidence produced inconclusive results. Occhicone's attorneys contended that his age-related health conditions — including kidney and prostate problems — could make lethal injection unusually painful, constituting cruel and unusual punishment. Supporters of capital punishment argue the executions deliver long-overdue justice; opponents contend the pace and the age and health of those executed raise serious constitutional and humanitarian concerns.

stories.headline: Uganda Declares Itself Ebola-Free as Congo Outbreak Becomes Fastest on Record
stories.summary:
Ugandan authorities declared the country free of Ebola on Tuesday after the last patient was discharged in mid-June and a mandatory 42-day monitoring period passed without evidence of further community transmission. Uganda's Ministry of Health confirmed that all identified contacts completed 21-day institutional quarantine and that enhanced surveillance detected no unexplained spread.

Uganda's outbreak was directly linked to a larger epidemic in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo, where the first confirmed Ugandan cases were Congolese nationals who crossed the border seeking treatment. Congo declared its outbreak on May 15; confirmed cases there have now reached 3,262 with 1,437 deaths, making it the fastest Ebola outbreak on record — and likely to surpass Congo's previous highest toll within days.

The Bundibugyo strain of Ebola responsible for this outbreak has no approved vaccine or treatment. The outbreak has been declared a global health emergency, and responders face mounting safety challenges in affected Congolese provinces, where rebel activity and community resistance have hampered tracing and isolation efforts deemed critical to halting spread.

Uganda's success was attributed to swift containment measures including suspension of public transportation and flights to Congo, mandatory quarantine protocols, and a presidential directive urging citizens to stop physical greetings. Public health officials cautioned that the risk of cross-border reintroduction remains as long as the Congo outbreak continues.

stories.headline: Update: Trump's New Tariffs on 80-Plus Countries Take Effect, Replacing Court-Struck Levies
stories.summary:
President Trump's new round of tariffs targeting more than 80 countries took effect Friday, imposing duties of either 10% or 12.5% on targeted nations based on their records on alleged forced labor violations. The move came on the same day a prior 10% global tariff — struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year — was set to expire, placing major tariff coverage on new legal footing.

The average U.S. tariff rate was 11.4% before the shift and fell slightly to 11.1% after the new levies replaced the temporary across-the-board tariff, according to the Yale Budget Lab. However, additional proposed tariffs are expected to push the average rate to 11.8% by the end of 2026. Trading partners affected by the new round account for approximately 99% of all U.S. imports, though product exemptions for some food, fuel, fertilizers, and USMCA-compliant goods will significantly reduce the practical impact.

Economists and analysts are divided on the consequences. Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid argued the announcement is 'less about raising tariff rates and more about preserving them,' noting little net economic change. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimated the tariffs could generate up to $900 billion in additional federal revenue over 10 years, helping incrementally reduce the national debt, though that figure is less than 60% of what the struck-down levies would have raised.

Critics warn the tariffs risk pushing up prices for household goods at a time when inflation is already elevated partly due to the ongoing Iran conflict. Supporters argue the policy restores American leverage in trade negotiations and puts tariff revenue on firm constitutional footing following the Supreme Court's earlier ruling.

stories.headline: Update: Trump and Netanyahu Meet at White House as U.S.-Iran Diplomacy Hangs in Dispute
stories.summary:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived at the White House Tuesday morning for high-stakes talks with President Donald Trump focused on the Iran conflict, Lebanon negotiations, and potential expansion of the Abraham Accords. The meeting comes amid growing friction between the two leaders, with Trump having publicly criticized Israel for continuing strikes in Lebanon and ignoring a ceasefire.

The diplomatic status of U.S.-Iran negotiations remains sharply contested. Trump told reporters that Iran had asked the U.S. to pause strikes and resume talks, saying Tehran 'asked us very nicely, please stop, let's meet.' Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman flatly contradicted that account, stating 'we have no negotiations with the United States at present,' while a deputy foreign minister denied any 'begging' by the Iranian side. Iran has separately engaged Oman in talks described as 'constructive' but 'unrelated' to U.S. negotiations.

Trump also met Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who described the session as a 'good meeting' covering Patriot missile interceptor licenses and renewed diplomatic efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Zelensky offered condolences on the day of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham's funeral and called for reinvigorating the diplomatic process. Iran has separately ramped up threats toward Kyiv following Ukraine's weekend strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea.

Oil markets continued to reflect the easing of immediate conflict fears, with Brent crude falling 2.9% Tuesday after dropping 11.3% Monday. Trump renewed threats to destroy Iranian bridges and power plants if no deal is reached, while the Pentagon faces questions about munitions stockpiles after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a Senate committee the department needs an additional $87 billion to address 'critical shortfalls.'

stories.headline: Magnitude 7.1 Earthquake Strikes Japan's Kyushu Island, Trapping People in Shopping Mall Collapse
stories.summary:
A magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Kumamoto prefecture on Japan's Kyushu island at 4:27 p.m. local time Tuesday, trapping an unknown number of people inside a collapsed Aeon Mall shopping center. The fire service reported contact had been lost with 20 to 30 employees at the mall, where the second floor collapsed and witnesses reported an explosion and smoke. Police are also investigating a paper factory where workers are reported missing after a chimney collapsed.

Approximately 300,000 residents have been directed to move to evacuation shelters. The quake caused power outages affecting more than 40,000 households, damaged roads, collapsed historic walls at the 17th-century Kumamoto Castle, and brought down a footbridge. More than 60 aftershocks ranging from magnitude 1 to 4 were recorded by Japan's Meteorological Agency. A tsunami warning issued immediately after the quake was lifted within two hours.

Kumamoto has significant earthquake history: a 7.3-magnitude quake in 2016 killed 278 people across Kumamoto and neighboring Oita prefectures and caused severe damage to the same castle now affected. The full toll of Tuesday's earthquake remains unclear as rescue and information-gathering operations are ongoing.

stories.headline: U.S. Delegation Walks Out of UN Security Council Meeting During French Remarks on Human Rights
stories.summary:
The United States delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting Monday in protest of comments by France's ambassador comparing U.S. voting behavior on human rights to that of authoritarian states. The confrontation originated when the U.S. joined Russia and North Korea in voting against extending the term of UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk, a vote that ultimately failed as 144 states approved Turk's reappointment.

France's UN mission had posted on X that 'The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore,' drawing a sharp rebuke from U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz, who accused Turk of 'lecturing' democracies while 'cozying up to the world's worst oppressors.' U.S. Ambassador Dan Negrea said the walkout would continue at future meetings until France 'renounces their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric.' The walkout occurred while France's ambassador was speaking during an emergency Security Council session on Russia's war in Ukraine.

The episode underscores deepening tensions between the Trump administration and United Nations institutions. The U.S. has cut funding for multiple UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of UN entities under the current administration. Following Friday's vote, U.S. Ambassador Jeff Bartos warned of 'consequences' and said Washington would 'immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding.' The UN's deputy spokesperson declined to comment on the walkout.

stories.headline: Update: Released Biden-Ghostwriter Audio Prompts Democratic Reckoning Over Hur Memory Claims
stories.summary:
Newly released audio recordings of former President Joe Biden speaking with memoir ghostwriter Mark Zwonitzer — released Monday following an FOIA battle — show Biden struggling to recall details and referencing classified information, corroborating key findings in Special Counsel Robert Hur's 2024 report. The tapes, recorded in 2016 and 2017, formed part of Hur's investigation into Biden's retention of classified documents, which concluded he had kept the materials but might be seen by a jury as 'a sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory.'

The release is drawing renewed scrutiny to prominent Democratic officials who aggressively challenged Hur's characterization of Biden's cognition at the time. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris called the report 'inaccurate and inappropriate' and said it was 'clearly politically motivated.' Rep. Dan Goldman described Hur as a Republican special counsel who 'completely went out of his way to editorialize.' Biden dropped out of the 2024 presidential race months after the report's release and was replaced on the ticket by Harris without a primary.

Supporters of Biden's position had argued that Hur, a Trump-era appointee, included gratuitous commentary beyond the scope of his investigative mandate, and that his conclusions about Biden's memory were politically colored. Critics contend the audio now confirms that concerns about Biden's fitness were substantiated and that Democratic officials misled the public. The episode continues to generate debate about Democratic Party accountability and the circumstances of Biden's exit from the 2024 race.

stories.headline: Kentucky Governor Demands McConnell Speak Publicly or Resign After 40-Day Absence
stories.summary:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) sent a formal letter Monday to Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and his staff demanding that the 84-year-old senator address constituents verbally to demonstrate his capacity to serve, or resign his seat. McConnell has not appeared in public since being hospitalized on June 14 for an unspecified medical condition — a stretch of more than 40 days. His office has released only written statements and two photographs during that period.

Beshear's letter represents the most direct public pressure yet on McConnell over his prolonged absence. The senator's office responded Monday with a health update stating he is still not ready to return to in-person work, but did not indicate a timeline for his return or address Beshear's resignation demand directly.

McConnell has experienced multiple health episodes in recent years, including a series of freezing episodes in 2023 that raised earlier questions about his fitness for office. As Senate Republican leader emeritus, his seat and health status carry implications for the Senate's partisan balance. Democrats argue the public has a right to know whether their senator can fulfill his duties; McConnell allies have historically pushed back on such demands as politically motivated.

Should McConnell resign or be unable to serve, Beshear as a Democratic governor would appoint his replacement — a dynamic that adds a partisan dimension to the governor's public ultimatum.

stories.headline: Concurrent Cyclospora and Salmonella Outbreaks Spread Across Multiple States, Raising Food Safety Alarms
stories.summary:
Two simultaneous foodborne illness outbreaks are straining U.S. public health resources. A cyclospora outbreak has produced nearly 4,200 confirmed cases across nine states, with thousands more unconfirmed, making it potentially the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak on record according to Johns Hopkins epidemiologist Caitlin Rivers. A separate salmonella outbreak linked to shelled eggs has sickened nearly 100 people across 17 states.

Rivers told PBS NewsHour that while one to two large foodborne illness outbreaks occur monthly in the U.S., the scale of the cyclospora outbreak is genuinely exceptional. The two outbreaks are caused by different pathogens and linked to different food sources, but share a common factor: the highly interconnected nature of the U.S. food supply, in which large producers distribute to millions of consumers across many states simultaneously.

Public health officials are still searching for the root source of the cyclospora cases, which have historically been linked to contaminated irrigation water on produce such as lettuce and berries. The salmonella outbreak's link to eggs is more straightforward but underscores ongoing vulnerabilities in the food safety system. Recent federal budget cuts to food safety inspection and oversight agencies have drawn scrutiny from public health advocates as the outbreaks widen.

The dual outbreaks come at a moment of heightened consumer concern about food safety and follow broader debates about staffing levels at the FDA and CDC after rounds of federal workforce reductions.

stories.headline: White Phosphorus Leak at U.S. Air Base Near Seoul Prompts Evacuation Order in South Korea
stories.summary:
South Korean authorities briefly ordered civilians to evacuate near Osan Air Base, a U.S. military installation located in Pyeongtaek south of Seoul, after what officials described as a white phosphorus leak detected around 5 p.m. local time Tuesday. City officials sent emergency text alerts urging residents within the affected area to move to safety and avoid skin exposure. The evacuation order was lifted several hours later after decontamination work was declared complete.

Police established a cordon of 300 to 500 meters around the base, blocking pedestrians and rerouting vehicle traffic. The U.S. 51st Fighter Wing issued a statement acknowledging a 'ground mishap' and confirming a 1,000-foot safety cordon, but did not confirm the specific substance involved, stating that reports of a general base evacuation were false. U.S. Forces Korea offered no further comment.

White phosphorus is a chemical compound used in incendiary munitions and smoke-generating ordnance. It ignites at high temperatures and can cause severe burns, making any uncontrolled release a serious hazard to civilians and military personnel alike. Its use in populated areas has been the subject of international controversy in various conflict contexts.

No major injuries or accidents were immediately reported. The incident highlights the sensitivities surrounding the large U.S. military presence in South Korea, where Osan Air Base is one of the primary American installations on the peninsula.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Blockades Strait of Hormuz as Iran Seizes Cargo Ships, Diplomacy Continues
stories.summary:
The United States has declared a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global shipping chokepoint, as the conflict with Iran enters a new phase. Iran has reacted by seizing two cargo ships in the strait, including the Epaminondas, with Tehran's foreign minister warning the assault on the vessel "cannot go unanswered." The U.S. military separately disabled a tanker attempting to evade the American blockade on Iranian ports.

Diplomatically, neither the U.S. nor Iran has launched direct strikes for three consecutive nights, following nearly two weeks of tit-for-tat attacks that threatened to derail peace negotiations. Iran's top negotiator has signaled that Tehran will "decide the right of passage" through Hormuz, while the new U.S. defense secretary has accused Iran and Russia of "sabre rattling." Iran also condemned a U.S. plan to use frozen Iranian assets to pay for war damages.

The conflict is producing significant economic ripple effects. Oil prices have returned to around $100 a barrel, and energy markets have experienced wild swings since the U.S. and Israel launched Operation Fury against Iran on February 28. In the UK, petrol and diesel prices are rising again, with Northern Ireland's Consumer Council directly attributing the increase to the conflict.

The human cost of the war continues to mount. An updated U.S. casualty figure now includes a new category called "Overseas Operations." Iran's Revolutionary Guard-linked groups have also issued warnings to the UK over allowing U.S. forces to use British bases for strikes on Iran. Five months after a strike killed 120 children in Minab in the war's opening hours, grief in that city remains raw.

stories.headline: ICE Launches Enforcement Operations in New York City, Targeting Queens and Long Island as Haitian TPS Expires
stories.summary:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement launched enforcement operations in New York City on Monday morning, beginning in Queens before shifting to Long Island on Tuesday, according to sources cited by NewsNation. The operations come on the same day that Temporary Protected Status for approximately 340,000 Haitian immigrants expired at 11:59 p.m. ET, rendering a large population immediately eligible for deportation.

The simultaneous expiration of TPS and the launch of targeted enforcement operations marks a significant escalation in immigration enforcement in one of the nation's largest cities. ICE is reportedly preparing a broader national blitz specifically targeting Haitian immigrants whose legal protections have lapsed, making Monday a pivotal date for that community.

Supporters of the administration argue that enforcing immigration law as TPS protections expire is legally straightforward and consistent with stated policy priorities. Critics contend that launching large-scale enforcement operations against a protected immigrant community on the precise day their status lapses is deliberately punitive and will create humanitarian crises for families with deep roots in the United States.

New York City has long maintained a sanctuary city posture, limiting local law enforcement cooperation with federal immigration authorities, which could complicate ICE operations on the ground. The scale and outcome of the enforcement actions are expected to be closely watched as a bellwether for similar operations nationwide.

stories.headline: Johnson & Johnson Offers Up to $5.5 Billion to Settle Baby Powder Cancer Lawsuits
stories.summary:
Johnson & Johnson has proposed paying as much as $5.5 billion to resolve approximately 76,000 lawsuits alleging that its talcum powder-based baby products caused ovarian cancer. The proposed settlement, announced Monday, would cover most of the remaining talc-related claims against the healthcare giant in both state and federal courts. J&J said it will offer up to $3 billion in the first payment next year, with additional amounts due no earlier than 2028.

The settlement must be accepted by legal firms representing at least 95 percent of the ovarian cancer claims before it can be finalized. J&J vice president of litigation Erik Haas maintained that the allegations are "meritless" and that the company was confident it would have "ultimately prevailed with further litigation," but chose to settle to put the matter behind it. The company stopped selling talc-based baby powder globally in 2022, transitioning to a cornstarch-based formula.

Lawsuits over J&J's talc products began as early as 2009, with plaintiffs alleging that asbestos contamination in the talc caused cancer. Talc is mined near asbestos deposits, a carcinogen. J&J has consistently denied its products contained asbestos or caused cancer, and earlier this month a federal court handed the company a significant victory by questioning individual plaintiffs' ability to prove causation.

The proposed $5.5 billion settlement, if finalized, would rank among the largest product liability resolutions in U.S. corporate history and would close a legal cloud that has hovered over the company for nearly two decades. J&J's former consumer health unit, Kenvue — which was spun off in 2022 and owns brands including Band-Aid and Listerine — holds liability for baby powder claims outside North America.

stories.headline: Update: Second Shooting at U.S. Consulate in Toronto This Year; Jewish Businesses Also Targeted Over Weekend
stories.summary:
A gunshot was fired at the U.S. consulate in Toronto early Monday morning, marking the second such attack on the facility this year. A police officer stationed outside the building heard a single shot and observed a white, license-plate-free car fleeing the scene. Officers briefly pursued the vehicle before ending the chase over safety concerns. No injuries were reported and at least two consulate staff inside the heavily fortified building were unharmed.

The new material development in this previously covered story is a widening pattern of targeted attacks on Jewish and American-linked sites in Toronto over the same weekend. Two Jewish-owned bakeries in the city were targeted by gunfire and vandalism, and while police said Monday there is currently no confirmed link between those incidents and the consulate shooting, they did not rule out a connection. The RCMP and international law enforcement partners have joined the investigation.

The March consulate shooting, to which this incident is being compared, was connected to a gun-for-hire network. Several suspects aged 18 and 19 were arrested in June for that attack. A Toronto police officer, Marc Pinizzotto, 43, was killed during raids related to that earlier investigation. Authorities have previously arrested an Iraqi national in the U.S. in connection with the consulate shooting pattern.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford called himself "totally disgusted" by the weekend's shootings and vandalism, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he was "appalled" and pledged full support for law enforcement. The incidents have renewed scrutiny of foreign interference and organized criminal networks operating in Canada, a subject of ongoing diplomatic sensitivity between Ottawa and Washington.
